A widower is a man whose wife has died. That is the heart of the word. It describes a specific marital status — not a divorced man, not a separated man, but a man whose wife is no longer alive.
The two conditions that must both be true

For a man to be called a widower, two things must be true at the same time:

  1. His wife has died.
  2. He has not married someone else after her death.

The moment he marries again, he is no longer a widower — he becomes a husband once more. However, you can still refer to his past status: "He was a widower for eight years before he remarried." That is perfectly correct.
Widower vs. Widow — the gender distinction

This is the single most important distinction to understand about this word.

  • Widow — a woman whose husband has died.
  • Widower — a man whose wife has died.

Same situation, different genders. English keeps them as two separate words. If you are ever unsure which is which, remember: widow is the older, shorter word (for the woman), and widower is the extended form (for the man).

In countries where same-sex marriages are legally recognized, the word naturally extends. A man whose husband has died is also called a widower. The defining factor is not the gender of the deceased spouse, but the gender of the surviving person. If the surviving person is a man, he is a widower. If the surviving person is a woman, she is a widow.

The word widowed is the adjective (and past participle) form of the same idea.

  • "He is a widower." (noun)
  • "He is widowed." (adjective)
  • "A widowed man sat by the window." (adjective modifying a noun)

All three mean essentially the same thing. Widowed can be used for both men and women, while widow and widower are gender-specific nouns.

• After his wife passed away, he became a widower at the age of fifty-two.
  • The widower raised his three children entirely on his own.
  • My grandfather was a widower for nearly two decades.
  • He had been a widower for five years when he finally met someone new.
  • The novel tells the story of a quiet, grief-stricken widower who slowly rediscovers life.

A widower is not just a legal or social label — the word carries the weight of loss. When you call someone a widower, you are implicitly acknowledging that he has experienced the death of his life partner. It is a word that sits at the intersection of love, marriage, and grief. In literature, films, and everyday conversation, widowers are often portrayed as people carrying a quiet sorrow, trying to rebuild their sense of self and purpose after an enormous loss.
The plural is simply widowers — no spelling change, just add an s. Example: Many widowers find it difficult to cook for themselves after years of shared meals.
A related expression worth knowing: "grass widow / grass widower"

This is an informal and somewhat old-fashioned expression. A grass widower is a man whose wife is away from him for a long period — not because she has died, but because of travel, work, or circumstance. The "grass" suggests a temporary, living separation, as opposed to the finality of death. This expression is rare in modern use, but you may encounter it in older literature. It is completely different in meaning from widower — the wife is alive; they are simply apart.
A widower is a man whose wife has died and who has not yet remarried — a word that marks both a marital status and, quietly, a profound human loss.
